title: The same brain, typed or spoken
subtitle: Why a spoken request and a typed request produce exactly one durable turn in the same conversation, and what it took to keep the two from drifting apart
technologies: Idempotency, exactly-once effects and crash recovery

stats.label: from a spoken request to the synthesiser admitting the quick opener
models: a light one keeps speech fast, the heavy brain does the work
identities: operator, employee, seat, voice session

lede: Talking to Helix and typing to Helix reach the same conversation and the same history. That sounds like a feature. It is a constraint, and it ruled out the obvious design. The obvious design points the voice engine's model endpoint at the control centre, so speech becomes just another client. I rejected it because it discards turn identity: the voice engine generates speculatively, retries, and interrupts, and each of those would have become a duplicate piece of durable work in the conversation. What I built instead is a control-only bridge. The voice engine keeps sole authority over audio and over the floor, who is speaking and who may interrupt.
quote: A spoken projection can never outrun the written answer.
evidence: Real-time voice AI: spoken and typed requests produce exactly one durable turn in the same conversation, and an interruption cancels that exact turn.
Latency engineering for voice AI: 699 ms from a spoken request to the synthesiser admitting the quick opener, with a light model keeping speech fast and a heavy one doing the work.
Identity separation in AI systems: operator, employee, seat and voice session kept as 4 identities that never merge, so each can change without touching the others.
author: Corey James
